paragraphs.text: Good evening, sisters and elders. I hope you had a great day today. I sure had a great day. Enjoyed visiting with the Baliuag and the Malolos districts, had all those district interviews, and they were great. Thank you to the members of those two districts because you made my day today.

Well, all right, in quantum physics, scientists are learning something really interesting, and that is that our futures are not set. They're not defined. They're not prescribed by our past. It doesn't matter where we were born. It doesn't matter the family we're born into. It doesn't matter any of those things in the past. According to quantum physics, our futures are simply endless possibilities that we actually determine by the way we think. Now, this has been something that's been talked about for hundreds, maybe thousands of years by philosophers and wise gurus, but now we have scientists talking about it that way. So literally, they're saying from one minute to the next minute, we're defining our futures by how we choose to think and decide on actions. I think that's amazing. So you literally can start in this moment and redefine your future by how you think in this moment and next moment and the moment after that. As you realize that this is true, and I hope you do, you'll begin to realize why it's so important that we think correctly. In fact, why we think according to the principles of God.

Now, the first real set, or really maybe defined set of godly principles that we know about and that the world knows about generally is found in the Ten Commandments. And almost everybody throughout the world has heard of the Ten Commandments. Two of these commandments are what I want to expand on in today's podcast, and I will add to those two commandments a third principle that if you combine it with the other two will make you a very unusual person who is honored by God and by everyone who knows you on earth and who has a future of the highest order of possibilities.

Now in giving the Ten Commandments, the Lord declared, "Thou shalt not steal," "Thou shalt not bear false witness." The Church's thirteenth article of faith states, "We believe in being honest." To be honest means to be sincere and truthful without deceit at all times. When we're honest in every way we are able to enjoy peace of mind and maintain our self-respect. We build strength of character which allows us to be of service to God and to others. We are trustworthy in the eyes of God and to those that we work with.

On the other hand, when we're dishonest in our words or our actions, we hurt ourselves every time and we often hurt others as well. If we lie, steal, cheat or neglect to give the full amount of work for our commitment and for our pay, we actually lose our own self-respect. We also lose the respect of others and we lose the guidance of the Holy Ghost. We may find that we have damaged relationships with family members or friends and that people no longer trust us.

Being honest often requires courage though, elders and sisters. It requires sacrifice especially when others try to persuade us to justify dishonest behavior. We may find ourselves in such a situation but the fact of the matter is we'll only find lasting peace when we sacrifice that desire to please those who would persuade us to do what's wrong and instead do the honest thing. That is far more valuable than following the crowd.

Let me tell you a story that happened to me and a friend of mine. I met this man when we were both about 12 years old. I had moved into the area and he was somebody that I immediately noticed was a person that was just a good person. We were never really super close friends but I always had respect for him because he was a straight shooter. He didn't do stuff dishonest. I didn't find him mocking those who were weaker than him. I didn't see him cheating on anything and as the years rolled by I just noticed that it just continued like that. We both graduated from high school the same year. He went on a mission. I went on a mission. We went our separate ways and I did not have any interaction with this man for about 25 years.

And then I got a phone call one day and it was this guy and he and I visited a little bit. It was nice to hear from him but I was kind of curious why was he calling me. And he said that he found some real estate that looked really good. Now I need to tell you he really understood real estate. This person, this guy, was actually buying real estate when he was still in high school. It wasn't very fancy real estate. It was really, really, you know, not expensive real estate but hey, the rest of us in high school we weren't doing anything like that. But here he was buying little old houses that he would fix up.

So he calls me this 25 years without having really heard from him and he says he's found a really nice set of apartments that he thinks is a great investment but he doesn't have enough money to buy them and he'd heard that, you know, I'd done pretty well in business and he said, "Would you be interested in investing with me?" And I said, "How much?" And he told me, and it was a lot of money. And I said, "Sure." And he says, "What do you need? What kind of contract? You have your lawyer call me and I'll sign whatever contract you want to write up." And I said, "I don't need a contract with you." He said, "You don't?" I said, "No, just tell me what your bank's numbers are and I'll send you the money." And he was really surprised by that. And I said, "Listen, I don't think that you would cheat me because you wouldn't be willing to do that to yourself."

Well, we went on and did millions of dollars of real estate, and quite successfully. And then one day he called me and he said, "I think the real estate market's at the top. I think we should sell everything and get out of it." I said, "Fair enough, go ahead and do it." And so he sold everything, he sent me my share, had done very well with him, we never had an agreement, never had a contract, nothing. Well, it reminds me of this quote from President Thomas S. Monson: "The surest test of an individual's integrity is his refusal to do or say anything that would damage his own self-respect." That's the way I felt about this man. I watched him grow up from a 12-year-old to a 25-year-old, I saw the way he behaved, and I knew that he would never do anything or say anything that would damage his own self-respect, and so I knew he would never cheat me.

Well, in Proverbs 20 verse 7 the Lord tells us, "The just man walketh in his integrity: his children are blessed after him." That's been the occasion that I've observed with this man. The book of Job in the Bible is full of wisdom. You know the story of Job; he was a very wealthy man with a great family, but then he lost his money and his family was lost also. Many people mocked him, many people thought he would blame God for his adversity and his tragedy, but instead he said this: "My lips shall not speak wickedness, nor my tongue utter deceit. God forbid that I should justify you: till I die I will not remove mine integrity from me."

In the Book of Mormon, we are inspired by the story of the stripling warriors. Their courage in battle and their faith in God was legendary. Their leader, the prophet Helaman, described them in a single sentence. He said, quote, "and they were all young men, and they were exceedingly valiant for courage, and also for strength and activity; but behold, this was not all—they were men who were true at all times in whatsoever thing they were entrusted," close quote. I would argue that that last part of that sentence is why that first part of that sentence is possible. If they were not men of integrity and men of honor, they wouldn't have been exceedingly valiant for courage.

Well, in Doctrine and Covenants section 124 verse 15 we read an interesting description of the Prophet Joseph Smith's brother, Hyrum Smith: "And again, verily I say unto you, blessed is my servant Hyrum Smith; for I, the Lord, love him because of the integrity of his heart." Integrity—the willingness and ability to live according to our beliefs and commitments. It is one of the foundation stones of good character, in fact I would argue it is the foundation stone of good character. You cannot hope to enjoy the presence of God, my dear elders and sisters, without integrity.

President Spencer W. Kimball says, quote, "Integrity is a state or quality of being complete, undivided, or unbroken. It is wholeness. It is purity and moral soundness. It is unadulterated genuineness and deep sincerity. It is courage, a human virtue of incalculable value. It is honesty, uprightness, and righteousness. Take these away and there is left but an empty shell. Integrity in individuals and in businesses or any organizations is not to ask, 'What will others think of me and my practices?' but rather, 'What do I think of myself if I do or don't do this thing? Is it proper? Is it right? Would the Master approve?' Integrity in a man should bring inner peace, sureness of purpose, and security in action. Lack of it," President Kimball goes on to say, "brings the reverse: disunity, fear, sorrow, unsureness, a lack of hope, a lack of faith, a lack of confidence."

"It would be well if all of us would take a frequent inventory to see if, hidden away under the rugs and in the corners of our lives, there might be some little vestige or piece of hypocrisy and ugliness or error. Or could there be hidden under the blankets of personal excuse or rationalization, some small dishonesties? Are there any cobwebs in the ceilings and corners which we think will not be noticed? Are we trying to cover up the small pettiness and the small gratifications we secretly allow in ourselves, rationalizing the while that they are just little and inconsequential? Are there areas of our thoughts and actions and attitudes which we would like to hide from those we respect the most?" close quote.

Dear elders and sisters, I ask each of you to ask yourselves these kinds of questions which President Spencer W. Kimball has posed to us in this call. It is good to do a regular inventory of our lives to make sure we are living with integrity. If we gain the whole world and lose our integrity, we will have nothing in the final day of judgment. Because all temporal values, all assets, all money, all properties, all these things will be left behind at death and the only thing we'll take with us will be our character, our attributes, and our intelligence. These are the things that will rise with us in the resurrection.

If you learn nothing else on your mission, I hope and pray that you will learn that the power to do what you say you're going to do, after the feeling has gone when you said it, will be your power. The power to do what's right and what you know is right, even when part of you does not want to do it or when people are telling you, "Don't worry about doing that." That power is the power that changes your life forever and pleases God. You want to be someone like Hyrum Smith, who the Lord is able to say, "and I, the Lord, love him because of the integrity of his heart." Have a good night, elders and sisters. I love you. I'm proud of you. I love the way you're continuing to grow and get better and stronger. Keep doing it. It's the process of perfection.
